The coffee was cold and Mr. Birch was still talking about the song on the radio, insisting it was about heroin and not about a woman at all, while Mr. Ash argued it was obviously about a woman who felt like heroin, and the waitress hovered with the check until Cal waved her off without a tip, saying she hadn't smiled once. Bram just watched them all like a man watching children argue over nothing, which in a way they were.

Elm was screaming and Ash held him against his chest in the dim warehouse, blood soaking through both their shirts, and Ash kept saying, over and over, you're not going to die, you hear me, you're not going to die, like the words themselves could seal the wound.

Birch came through the door with the diamonds in a gym bag and his face gray with fury, saying somebody had known, somebody had told the cops exactly where and when, and he wasn't leaving them lying around for anyone to find, so he took the bag back out into the dark and buried it where only he would know.

Earlier, before any of it — before the job even had a shape — Bram had stood in the kitchen of the safehouse and handed out the names like a man dealing cards. Birch had made a face. Why do I have to be Birch, he'd said, I don't even like trees. Bram told him to shut up and be grateful he wasn't Mr. Cedar.

And Cedar arrived that morning grinning, popped the trunk of his car, and there was a cop inside, wrists zip-tied, mouth taped, eyes huge with terror. His name, it turned out, was Doyle.

Before that, weeks before, Ren Vasco had walked out through the prison gates into gray daylight and gone straight to Bram and Cal, reminding them without needing to say much that he'd done years and kept his mouth shut the whole time, and that debts like that got paid.

Left alone with Doyle in a back room, Cedar turned on an oldies station, danced a little to it with his eyes closed, then took a knife to the man's ear while Doyle screamed into the tape, and poured gasoline over him like it was a joke he was building toward.

Elm shot him from the floor before the match ever came. Blood on the tile, ringing in his ears. He crawled to Doyle and told him he was a cop, that this whole thing was a setup, and that officers were outside waiting for Bram to show his face.

Before any of that, in a gray little office, Pruitt had made him tell the toilet-bust story again and again until it sounded like something he remembered instead of something written for him, until his voice stopped shaking.

Then he told it for real — to Bram, to Cal, to Ash — and they laughed in the right places, and Bram clapped him on the shoulder and told him welcome aboard, Mr. Elm.

The robbery lasted less than a minute before it came apart, and Ash drove them out under fire, gun out the window, screaming at Elm to get down.

On foot, Elm flagged a car at a light, and the driver, panicking, put a bullet in his stomach; Elm shot him through the seat before the man could pull away.

Cal came back into the warehouse, listened to Elm's account of Cedar's death, then shot Doyle where he sat without a word.

Bram arrived last, looked at Elm, and said the word informer like a verdict. Ash wouldn't have it, turned his gun on Bram instead.

The three of them fired at once, and by the time it stopped Bram and Cal were dead on the concrete and Ash was on his knees, gut-shot, still breathing.

Elm said it then, finally — I'm a cop — and Ash raised his gun and put a bullet through him just as the doors burst open and the light came pouring in, and then Ash went down too, under a hail of fire, still not believing any of it.

The old man died alone in the echoing hall of Silvermount, the marble floor throwing back a hundred versions of the lamplight, and the last word he spoke was "Bluebell." The glass globe slipped from his hand and rolled a little way before it stopped, and no one was there to hear what he meant.

The newsreels ran the story that week with brass fanfare and a somber narrator: Emmett Rusk, press baron, philanthropist, twice-married, builder of the unfinished palace where he'd died. They showed the Clarion's masthead, the ruins of his political ambitions, footage of a young woman singing badly in an opera house. The reel ended on his name in block letters. It never explained the word.

So the paper sent a young reporter named Nash to find out. He tracked down a nightclub on the coast where a woman drank alone most nights, and when he said Rusk's name to her she called him a fool and had him thrown into the street before he could ask about Bluebell.

He went further back than that. He read Barrow's memoir first — the old banker's account of a defaulted mining claim, a mother in a boarding house signing over her son once the family struck it rich by another man's ruin. Barrow wrote of the boy who drove a sled into his stomach rather than leave, and how he'd taken him east anyway, deed and all.

On his twenty-fifth birthday, Emmett had walked into Barrow's office and asked, of all the properties in his inheritance, for a failing newspaper called the Clarion. He moved into its offices, brought in Marsh to manage the books and Devlin to write, and printed a signed statement of principles above the fold. Then he hired away the entire staff of the rival paper and threw them all a party with a brass band and a chorus line, as if journalism were only another kind of conquest.

He came home from Europe engaged to Adele, the governor's niece, and for a while the marriage looked like triumph. Then came years of breakfasts eaten behind separate newspapers, the silence thickening like scum on cooling soup. One muddy afternoon he met a shopgirl named Nora Kell on the street and began visiting her rooms, quietly, the way men visit things they mean to keep secret.

Halloran, the party boss, found out mid-campaign and brought Adele to Nora's door to threaten exposure. Emmett refused to withdraw from the race and lost anyway. Devlin asked for a transfer. The marriage ended in paperwork and silence.

Drunk one night, Devlin began writing the review that savaged Nora's operatic debut — a career Emmett had forced on her though she had no voice for it — and Emmett, sober, finished it, printed it, and fired his oldest friend for the words they'd both written. He'd already married Nora by then, made her sing before she collapsed and swallowed poison rather than go onstage again. He let her stop, finally, once it nearly killed her.

He shut her away instead, in the half-built palace called Silvermount, where she spent her days assembling jigsaw puzzles in a hall built for parties that never came. A picnic on the beach ended in a quarrel neither of them survived; she packed her things and left him. He wrecked her bedroom afterward, searching for something, and found instead a glass snow globe on her dresser. "Bluebell," he murmured, and carried it past the mirrored walls.

Nash gathered all of this — Barrow's pages, Marsh's ledgers, Devlin's bitterness, Nora's refusal, the butler Colm's quiet testimony — and understood, finally, that no single word could hold a man's whole life. Outside the empty house, workmen were clearing the grounds, and among the debris they found a child's sled, paint faded, the name Bluebell still legible on its side, and fed it to the furnace without a second look.

Aaron bought the gun three days before he ever explained to anyone why. He had already decided that Wes Tarrow would die at the motel off the interstate, and the decision felt, in his ruined chest, like the only mathematics he had left.

Wes had once been a man who coached boys' baseball in the evenings, who quoted scripture at the dinner table until his wife Nita flinched, who held down a job at the plant and told himself he had been made new. He did not know, then, that he would ever be tracked to a motel by a man carrying his victim's heart.

Lena, in those same lost years, had lived in a house with a green door, married to Doug, mother to two girls who fought over the radio in the back seat. She had been clean four years. She thought that counted for something.

Aaron himself had once been only a mathematician who could not breathe. A doctor had told him, without ceremony, that his heart would fail within weeks, and that unless a stranger died in time, so would he.

After the funerals, Lena went back to the powder and the spoon with the patience of someone finishing an unfinished task. She was not trying to feel better. She was trying to stop.

The crossing where it happened had a stop sign nobody obeyed. Wes's truck came through too fast, struck Doug and both girls, and he drove on, then turned back, then fled a second time, leaving the intersection empty and ringing.

Aaron, meanwhile, had married Della years before any of this, and near the end of his life she had pressed a vial of frozen sperm into his hand and asked him to let her keep something of him, whatever was left, growing inside her when he was gone.

At the hospital, a nurse told Lena that her husband and both her daughters were dead, using the flat voice reserved for the worst sentences.

Wes walked into a police station not long after and confessed, unprompted, to a hit-and-run, and the courts sent him back to the cell he had only just left behind.

Doug's heart, still warm enough to matter, went into Aaron's chest that same week, and Aaron woke from the surgery astonished simply to be breathing.

He could not stop thinking about the person to whom that beating muscle had belonged, and so he hired a private investigator to find the widow.

Wes was released early for good behavior he did not feel he possessed, and he left Nita standing in the driveway with the screen door swinging, and drove until he found a motel that would give a friendless man work.

Aaron found Lena first. He arranged a meeting at a public pool, let her think it was chance, and let the affair begin in the flat unhurried light of afternoons neither of them examined too closely.

He left Della not long after, telling her plainly that he did not want the child she was carrying toward on his behalf, that he had no more claim to give.

At the motel, when Aaron finally raised the gun, his hand would not finish what his mind had decided; he shot Wes once, low, and told him to run while he still could.

Before that, in Lena's kitchen, Aaron had confessed what he carried in his chest, and she had put him out into the street and then, within days, let him back in, as if his heart were a debt she alone could collect.

Wes did not run far. He followed them back to their own motel room and asked Aaron, quietly, to finish what he'd started. Aaron turned the gun on himself instead.

Lena and Wes carried him together to the hospital, where the borrowed heart, Doug's heart, finally stopped for good. Wes went home to whatever family would still have him. Lena, pregnant, drove home alone, past the crossing, past the stop sign nobody obeyed, into a house that no longer had anyone left to fill it.

Tobias skipped work on an impulse he couldn't name, took the train to the end of the line where the town met the sea, and found a woman standing on the frozen sand as if she'd been waiting for him specifically, though neither of them could have said why. Her name was Ivy. They talked until the cold drove them off the beach, and then they drove back to the city together, her hand loose on the gearshift, and she invited him up to her flat like it was the easiest thing in the world.

Weeks later he went to the bookshop where she worked and she looked at him like a customer, polite and empty, laughing at something a young man named Peck said to her over the register. Tobias stood in the poetry aisle for a long time before he left.

Nina and Grady showed him the letter — a form letter, clinical and bloodless, thanking a patient for choosing their memory-erasure service. He recognized Ivy's name typed at the top. He went straight to the clinic and stood in front of Dr. Hallam's desk and said, do it to me too, take all of it.

He spent the following days boxing up everything that had her fingerprints on it — a scarf, ticket stubs, a chipped mug — laying the objects out so the technicians could map what memories clung to them. Two men came that night, Dell and the same Peck from the bookshop, running cables and murmuring to each other in the dark of his flat. Peck slipped a few of the smaller mementos into his jacket pocket when he thought no one was looking.

Inside his own skull, Tobias watched the ugliest, most recent memories go first — the dent in the car, her voice slurred and vicious, the door slamming. He watched himself hurl accusations at her about the drinking, watched her hurl back his silences, his refusal to ever say what he meant. He watched her leave for good, watched the fight replay and dissolve, replay and dissolve.

Down in the flat, Dell and a receptionist named Rosa got high on his bed and lost the thread of the procedure entirely, and the map began sliding sideways, memories bleeding into each other. When he reached the ones he actually loved, Tobias balked. He started dragging Ivy into memories she'd never been part of — birthdays, a childhood dog, rooms she'd never stood in — trying to hide her somewhere the erasure wouldn't find her.

They had two good years before any of that. The frozen river where they'd first kissed, the noodle house with the cracked red booths, the drive-in where they fell asleep before the second feature. All of it good, once, before the drinking and the withholding turned it to rot.

Dr. Hallam himself came to fix the collapsing map, and Rosa, still glassy-eyed, kissed him without thinking — until his wife arrived and told her, flatly, that this wasn't the first time, that Rosa's own affair with him had already been erased once before, by his own clinic, on his own orders.

Before any of it — the erasure, the rot, the years — there was a beach party in that same seaside town, and a house standing empty on the shore, and Tobias and Ivy breaking a window latch to get inside, laughing at their own daring.

That house was the last memory left standing. In it, they said goodbye, and she told him to meet her at the beach.

Then it was morning. He woke with no memory that she had ever existed at all.

Later, Rosa quit the clinic in disgust and mailed every patient their files and session tapes, unopened, unedited.

Tobias and Ivy sat together and listened to their own recorded voices tearing each other apart, ugly and small. She ran. She came back. Neither of them explained it. They just agreed, quietly, to try anyway.

The photograph developed slowly in Martin's hand, the chemical smell still sharp in the derelict room. Roy Mercer lay on the concrete, one eye open, blood pooling black in the dim light. Martin didn't feel anything looking at it. He never did, for long. He wrote *ROY. DONE.* on the white border and slid it into his jacket.

In the motel room, the phone cord stretched taut across his knuckles. "I don't know how I got here," Martin said to the voice on the other end. "But I remember the Prine case fine. Elias Prine came to me with memory loss, wanted a payout for a head injury. I ruled it psychosomatic. Denied the claim." He said it flatly, a man reciting a case file, unaware he was reciting his own shape.

Corinne sat across a scarred desk at the vehicle registry two days earlier, watching her friend type the plate number Martin had given her. The printout came back a name: *Roy Mercer.* She folded it once and put it in her purse like a blade.

Years before any of this, Martin sat across a conference table from Elias Prine, watching the man's hands shake. "There's no clinical basis for what you're describing," Martin told him, and stamped the folder DENIED.

In a motel bathroom, Martin pressed a gun into Vance's ribs and marched him, dripping blood from a split lip, out to the parking lot. "Get in the car," Martin said. "You're leaving town tonight."

Elias's wife lay in the bed, insulin vial in his shaking hand. "One more," she whispered, testing him, and he gave it, forgetting the last one, and the one before that, until her heart gave out beneath the sheets.

Corinne came home with a bruise blooming under her eye, blaming Vance, though she had goaded Martin's fist there herself, hiding every pen in the house first so he could write nothing down to contradict her story later.

Martin built his system on a motel wall: photographs pinned in rows, notes in his own cramped hand, the tattoos on his arms and thighs cataloguing facts he could not otherwise keep. FACT ONE. FACT TWO. R.M. — the man who took his memory, who he was hunting through the only archive he trusted: his own skin.

At her bar, Corinne wiped down glasses and watched the man in Gil's suit drink a beer her staff had spat in, not knowing yet how much he'd forgotten, only that he was wearing a dead man's clothes and driving a dead man's car.

In his bathroom at home, intruders came through the frosted glass and the steam. Martin killed one with a broken bottle; the second cracked something loose in his skull that never healed right again.

At a tattoo parlor lit by buzzing fluorescents, Martin had a license plate inked into his thigh, sixth in the sequence, the needle biting deeper than he'd admit.

He burned his wife's hairbrush in a field, the bristles curling to ash, and could not remember, moments later, why his hands smelled of smoke or why his face was wet.

The caller on the phone gave him a name — Gil Marsh — and an address, and told him this was the man he'd been circling for a year.

Martin beat Gil in a basement that smelled of rust and mildew until the man stopped moving, and photographed the body the way he photographed everything now, for later, for proof.

Gil's last word was "Elias," a name that meant nothing and everything, and Martin took his suit, his keys, his car.

Roy found him there and told him the truth — that Gil was innocent, that the real man was dead a year already, that Martin himself was the Prine in every story he'd been telling.

A year earlier, that same Roy had stood beside him at the real killing, watched Martin do what needed doing, and watched him forget it within minutes, as he forgot everything.

Martin burned Gil's photographs in the sink and wrote across Roy's picture, in block letters: HE IS LYING TO YOU. He copied the plate number down before the ink of memory failed him again.

The two men in the vinyl booth had been talking about rent for twenty minutes before one of them, the younger one with the bad haircut, said "we should just take this place" like he was suggesting they order pie. His partner blinked at him, then nodded slow, like the idea had been sitting in his own head the whole time waiting for someone else to say it out loud. Neither of them had planned past that sentence.

Rollo and Marcus were crossing the bridge into the industrial side of town, windows down, arguing about what they call a Quarter Pounder in countries that don't use quarters. "They just call it the Royale," Marcus said. "That's not a translation, that's a whole different name." Rollo said something about hash being legal in certain places and Marcus said that didn't mean it was smart, and the argument went nowhere, the way their arguments always did, all the way to the corridor outside Tobin's door, where they lowered their voices and kept arguing anyway — this time about whether Marcus's girlfriend's foot massages were worth what they were about to do for a man like Otis. "Everything's worth something," Marcus said, and knocked.

Inside, Marcus said a few lines that sounded like scripture, and then the gun did the rest, and Tobin sat down hard against the wall he'd been leaning near a second before. They took the briefcase off the table like it belonged to them.

They brought it to Otis at the bar, where Otis was leaning over a stool talking dollar figures into the ear of an old boxer named Denny, telling him the fifth round, telling him it wouldn't hurt his record any more than his knees already had. Otis took the briefcase without looking inside it and told the two men to enjoy the rest of their night.

Rollo enjoyed his by finding Kip and pushing a needle into the crook of his arm before he even changed his shirt. Loose and warm, he took Nadia — Otis's wife — to the diner done up like the fifties, and they won the dance contest under a paper banner, spinning until the other couples gave up. Later, on Kip's floor, Nadia's lips went the color of a candle flame just before it dies, and it took an adrenaline needle straight into her chest to bring her back gasping.

Long before any of that, Denny had been a boy standing in a doorway while a soldier just off a ship pressed a gold watch into his hand and said his father had kept it through years in a cage overseas. Denny had worn it every day since like a second pulse.

In the fifth round he didn't go down. He put his opponent down instead, for good, and left the ring in a stolen taxi. In the motel, Marielle told him she'd left the watch behind on the dresser, and something in his face closed like a door.

He went back for it. Rollo was still in the kitchen, loose-limbed from the night before, and never got a hand near the machine gun on the counter before Denny used it.

Denny and Otis found each other in the street by accident, a screech of metal, and woke up chained in a pawnshop basement. When one of their captors turned his attention to Otis in the worst way, Denny got free of his ropes and came off the wall with a sword still in its display sheath. Otis, bleeding, called them square, so long as Denny rode out of the city.

Weeks earlier, back before any of that, a fourth man had jumped from Tobin's bathroom and emptied a revolver at Rollo and Marcus without touching either of them, and Marcus had thanked God out loud for it in the car, right up until his own gun went off by accident and took the head off their passenger Del.

They'd driven the ruined car to Warren's house, where a man with a hose and a bag of clean shirts told them where to stand and what to burn.

And once, in a coffee shop robbery gone sideways, Marcus had talked a nervous kid down with his own wallet in his hand, kept the briefcase, and watched the doors swing shut on two people who'd live to rob somewhere else.

Denny found Marielle, and they took a motorcycle off the pawnshop floor, and rode until the city was just a haze of taillights behind them, his father's watch ticking against his wrist the whole way out.

The old man's window looked down on the street where the flashing lights still turned the wet pavement blue and red. He had lit his pipe before starting to speak, and now let it go out between his fingers.

"Nothing survives," he said. "You understand that. Bone, love, cities. Given time enough."

The younger man, who had been made to sit and listen though every part of him wanted to be elsewhere, watched the police below shoving two handcuffed figures into a car.

"Look at those two," the old man said. "Whatever they did tonight, in fifty years it will be dust in a record nobody reads."

Below, Cort and Jonah were dragged out of the club into the open air, wrists bound, faces bloodied, blinking at the crowd that had gathered to watch. Neither of them said anything. There was nothing left in either man that wanted to speak.

Minutes before, Jonah had been standing over a stranger with a fire extinguisher in his hands, bringing it down again and again into a face that had stopped being a face, while a few feet off, unnoticed, unbothered, the man they called the Adder leaned against the wall and watched with mild interest, as though at a fight he had no stake in.

Before that, Cort had shoved through the crush of bodies inside the Pit, seized a man by the collar — the wrong man, some stranger with the wrong haircut and the wrong luck — and wrenched his arm back until it broke with a sound like a branch giving way.

Before that, two men on the street outside had sidled up to Cort and Jonah with quiet, ugly smiles, telling them they knew a name, they knew where to find him, if the price was right, and they had walked them toward the doors of the club, laughing softly to each other the whole way.

Before that, Cort and Jonah had come stumbling out of the party's noise and light to find Lise being lifted onto a stretcher, her face slack, blood already darkening in her hair, paramedics moving around her with the brisk indifference of men who had seen this before.

Before that, in the underpass, the Adder had held her down and forced himself into her, and when she fought he had taken her skull in his hand and driven it against the concrete, once, twice, while somewhere behind them a man walking home glanced in, understood exactly what he was seeing, and kept walking.

Before that, she'd taken the underpass instead of crossing the road, and found the Adder there already, beating a transsexual woman against the wall with a kind of bored cruelty, and Lise had frozen half a second too long in the entrance.

Before that, in the party's overheated rooms, Cort had gotten steadily drunker, then higher, until he was trailing after other women with his hand out, and Lise had watched him do it for the length of one drink before she put her coat on and walked out alone.

Before that, the three of them — Lise, Cort, Jonah — had ridden the underground together, laughing, arguing about sex and about how much Cort drank, the carriage rattling under the city, none of them yet knowing what the night held.

Before that, in bed, Lise had described to Cort a dream she kept having, a tunnel and a red light at the end of it, and they had teased each other lazily about Jonah, about old feelings, none of it serious.

Before that, alone in the flat one afternoon, she had taken a test and watched the line appear, and sat very still for a long time afterward.

And before that — after all of it, really, though she did not think of it that way — she sat in a park in the sun, sprinklers turning lazy arcs over children's shouting, a book open on her lap, one hand resting, without her quite noticing, on the small curve of her stomach.

The call came at 4 a.m., and Detective Isaiah Reece drove out to the shoulder of the frontage road with his coffee going cold in the cupholder, thinking it was just another body until he pulled back the sheet and found his brother's face underneath it, gray and unmarked except for the burn along one arm. He would remember, standing there, that he had not looked for Kwame in three years. That moment sat behind everything else, though the world did not yet know to wait for it.

Weeks earlier, in the part of the story that still made sense in order, Nadir stood at a gun counter with his daughter Sahar while the dealer repeated his broken English back to him in a mocking sing-song, sliding the pistol across the counter like a favor he hadn't earned. Across town, two young men named Trey and Kwame put a gun to the window of a car outside a restaurant and took it from a prosecutor named Halstead, who stood on the curb after with his hands still raised.

Days after that, a locksmith named Mateo came to the Halstead house to change the locks, and Paula stood in her doorway insisting loudly to her husband that the boy was probably in a gang, going to sell copies of the keys to his friends. Mateo said nothing and did his work.

Around the same week, a patrolman named Boyle pulled over a black couple, the Hobarts, on a dark road and put his hands on Renee in front of her husband Clay before letting them go with a warning that meant nothing. His partner Voss watched from the passenger seat and said nothing that night, but soon after asked their commander for a new partner, unable to stomach another shift beside him.

Mateo went next to Nadir's shop to replace a broken lock, warning him plainly that the door itself was rotten and needed fixing, and Nadir, suspicious of everyone by now, accused him of running a scam. Not long after, Boyle knelt in an insurance office begging a clerk named Delia Frank to approve treatment for his dying father, and she told him, without unkindness, that there was nothing she could do. That same season, Nadir's shop was gutted overnight, glass everywhere, and the insurer refused to pay him a cent, citing the door he'd never fixed.

Trey and Kwame, still running together, ran down a shopkeeper named Pham with their car and left him outside the hospital doors like an offering. Not far away, Renee was upside down in a wreck, flames licking at the frame, and it was Boyle — that same Boyle — who crawled in and pulled her out.

Then Clay, caught in the act of stealing back his own car from the impound after all of it, was nearly shot until Voss talked the other officers down. Later, fleeing the police in that same car, Clay drove wild and finally threw Trey out onto the pavement.

Nadir, certain now of what the world had done to him, waited outside Mateo's house with his gun and fired the moment little Rosie ran laughing into her father's arms. But no one fell — Sahar had loaded the gun with blanks, and Nadir wept and called the child his angel.

Not long after, Voss picked up a hitchhiker who turned out to be Kwame, misread his hand moving toward his pocket, and shot him where he stood, then set the car alight to hide it. This was the body Reece would find, the body that had already appeared at the start.

His mother, when he told her, said only that he had never once gone looking for his brother, and he had no answer.

Paula fell down her own staircase soon after and told her housekeeper Alba, gripping her hand, that she was the only friend she had left. Trey, alone now, found Pham's van full of trafficked people at the edge of the docks and let them all go into the dark rather than sell them onward.

And in the first snow of that year, two cars touched bumpers on an ordinary street, and the shouting started again, as it always did.

The gun tasted like a battery, copper and acid, and when I pulled the trigger the cheek opened like a door I'd been trying to find for years. I want you to understand this before anything else, because everything that follows only makes sense once you know how it ends: I am standing in a stairwell with a hole in my face, and the man who put me there is falling out of me like water out of a cracked glass.

But that's later. Let me back up.

For a long time the only thing that worked was crying. I'd sit in folding chairs in church basements, hand on a stranger's knee, and sob about diseases I did not have, and afterward I'd sleep four hours instead of none. It was the only medicine that took.

Then Ada Vey started showing up. She faked it worse than I did—dry eyes, a catch in her voice she'd clearly practiced—and just by being there she ruined it for me. I couldn't cry with a fraud in the room. I stopped sleeping again.

On a flight to a recall hearing I sat next to a soap salesman named Rex Marrow. Good suit, terrible shoes. He gave me his card and I put it in my pocket and forgot him, the way you forget everyone on a plane.

My apartment exploded. All my catalogue furniture, gone, a grease fire that ate a whole floor. I called the only number I had. Rex met me at a derelict house on the edge of the industrial district and told me I could stay.

Outside a bar one night he asked me to hit him as hard as I could. I did. He hit me back. We went home looking like meat.

It became a thing we did on Tuesdays, in the basement, and then other men wanted in, and then it wasn't two men anymore, it was a room full of men taking turns being ruined.

Ada overdosed and Rex carried her in from wherever he'd found her, and after that they were together, loud about it, laughing through walls at three in the morning while I lay there with my ears full of blood.

Rex had a side business: fat skimmed from cosmetic surgery clinics, rendered into soap, sold back to department stores for eighty dollars a bar. He thought it was funny. Rich women paying to buy back their own thighs.

One night he held my hand against a bar of lye until it blistered, wouldn't let me close my eyes and float away like I usually did. "Stay here," he said. "Stay in it."

I went to my employer with my face still wrecked and told them to pay me to disappear or explain the photographs. They paid.

Rex built the basement into something bigger. He called it Havoc. Boys with shaved heads slept in the house and took orders and went out at night to break things that belonged to banks.

Then he drove us into oncoming traffic, let the car roll twice, and when I crawled out he was gone. Not dead. Just gone.

A recruit named Ogden got shot on a job and I decided, standing over the sheet they put him under, that I would end the whole thing.

I traveled. City after city, identical basements, identical shaved boys, and every one of them called me Rex Marrow when I walked in.

It took longer than it should have to understand why.

Ada told me plainly, no cruelty in it: she had never been sleeping with someone else. She had been sleeping with me the whole time. Rex woke up when I went under.

Havoc had wired the debt-record towers with charges, floor by floor, and I went in alone to cut wires with hands that weren't sure whose they were.

Which brings us back to the stairwell, the beating, the gun, the door I opened in my own face to let the other man bleed out of it.

The shaved boys brought Ada to the tower afterward, past the smoke, up through the stairwell where I was still standing. We held hands at the window. Below us the buildings came down one after another, patient as a countdown, and for once, watching it, I didn't need to cry to feel my chest go quiet.

Solly Two Coats and his crew went into the northern diamond house dressed as pilgrims, murmuring prayers with their hats low, and walked out with a stone the size of a knuckle. Nobody looked twice at devout men.

Meanwhile, overseas, Halloway and Digby sent their fighter Pretty Sam down to a camp of travellers to buy a caravan for the show. Sam offered a low price and got a low answer: the bare-knuckle man Finn put him on the ground and left him there sleeping in the mud. Halloway had no fighter now, and the fixed bout for the gang boss Coldstone was two days off.

Solly's cousin Marv rang him from overseas and told him to bring the stone straight over, no detours, no cleverness. Solly said he'd come. Halloway, meanwhile, had no choice but to put Finn in himself, and swore to Coldstone that the man would go down clean in the fourth.

Back in the city, Grigor the Nail heard whispers of a bookmaker's shop worth robbing, and in the same breath told the pawnbrokers Ike and Benno where to find it, setting two hungry dogs on the same bone without either knowing.

Solly landed with the stone stitched into his lining, handed it to the fence Hersch for holding, and went off to the bookmaker's to put money on Finn.

Finn, in the ring, put his man down cold in the very first round — no fourth, no arrangement — and Coldstone lost a fortune he meant to keep, and turned his rage on Halloway like a dog on a leash finally let go.

At the bookmaker's, Ike, Benno and Tulley bungled their robbery, grabbed Solly's arm and his case in the scramble, and fled with Grigor's men hard on their heels through the wet streets.

Marv flew in to find his cousin gone and the stone with him, and hired the bounty hunter Ledge, a man who did not miss.

Grigor found Solly first. He took the arm off him to get at the case, and inside there was no stone at all — just paper, sweat, and Solly's ruined arm on the table.

Coldstone, still burning, fed what was left of Solly to his pigs, and told Halloway and Digby plainly what would happen to them if the next fight went the same crooked way as the last.

Ledge, patient and thorough, traced the pawnbrokers to a back road, put their car through with gunfire, and took Ike, Benno, and the stone all at once.

Halloway and Digby told Finn again — down in the fourth, no mistakes this time — and that same night Coldstone's men burned Finn's mother alive in her caravan to make sure he understood the stakes.

Grigor, still hunting, ambushed Ledge's car with Ike and Benno trapped inside, and in the crossfire Ledge, Grigor, and Benno all went down together in the dirt.

Tulley, forgotten in the chaos, slipped away with the dog — the dog that had swallowed the diamond whole days before, unnoticed by anyone.

Finn climbed into the ring with his mother's ashes still warm and knocked his man out in the fourth exactly as told, and in the stands the travellers rose up and tore through Coldstone's men like a reckoning long overdue.

Halloway and Digby, seeing their chance, found Coldstone cowering and shot him where he stood. By morning the travellers had folded their camp and vanished as if they'd never been.

Weeks later, a dog was handed in at a pet shop, sickly and coughing, and brought up a diamond onto the counter in front of two stunned men. Halloway and Digby stood there holding it, the whole bloody chain of it behind them, and neither one said a word.

All night the helicopters moved over the city like slow insects, spraying for the pests that had gotten into the crops that ringed the suburbs, their lights sliding across rooftop after rooftop, missing no one.

In one of those houses, Neil Hartigan buttoned his shirt while his wife Bess stood at the mirror deciding on earrings, the two of them getting ready for a dinner party they'd already half-regretted agreeing to host.

Across town, in a dim living room lit by one lamp, Cheryl murmured into a telephone receiver, walking a stranger through his fantasy in a low, practiced voice, while her husband Stu sat a few feet away, saying nothing, his jaw tight with something he wouldn't name.

In another house a cello leaned against a chair, untouched most nights until Bee picked it up alone, filling the empty rooms with sound while her mother, the singer Vida, performed under lights at the club, night after night, for people who weren't her daughter.

Officer Rowe told his wife Peg he had to work late again. He was really going to see Nan. On his way out he left the family dog tied to a post two streets over, telling himself he'd come back for it, knowing he wouldn't.

That same morning, a boy named Charlie Rill was walking to school when a car driven by a waitress named Rhona clipped him at the corner. He got up, brushed off his knees, and told everyone at home that he was fine.

Days earlier, the baker Otto Kemp had written down an order: a birthday cake, the name Charlie Rill, a date circled on the calendar.

Now Charlie lay still in a hospital bed, sunk into a coma no one could explain, and his parents Grant and Elaine sat in plastic chairs keeping vigil under fluorescent light.

Meanwhile, in the Hartigans' empty house, the sitters Ike and Dot amused themselves: Dot lay across the guest bed made up like a corpse, bruises painted onto her throat, while Ike photographed her, laughing at how convincing it looked.

Out on the river, Stu and three friends found a young woman floating face down in the current, her hair fanned out like something painted.

Not far off, Nan's ex-husband Cass, a helicopter pilot who flew the same routes that sprayed the city at night, learned she had a new man and went to her house with a saw, and took her furniture apart piece by piece.

Otto Kemp, unpaid for the cake, ignored when he called to ask after it, began phoning the Rill house at odd hours, saying nothing, or saying something worse than nothing.

Stu and his friends tied the woman's body to a root at the bank and kept fishing for two more days before anyone called the police.

At the hospital, Grant's father Duff, a man Grant hadn't spoken to in years, appeared in the waiting room and, unasked, confessed an affair from decades before, as though this were the moment for it.

Vern's wife Iris, a party clown still in her makeup from a child's birthday, heard what the men had done with the body and could not look at her husband for days.

At the dinner party, wine loosening everyone's tongue, Bess admitted to a nude modeling session years ago, and then to an affair, and Neil stood up so fast his chair fell backward.

Charlie died that night. Grant and Elaine drove to the bakery afterward, meaning to accuse Otto of something, but instead sat while he pulled warm bread from the oven and wept with them, wordless.

At home, Vida found her daughter Bee asleep, or so it seemed, and did not know until it was too late that Bee had closed the garage door and let the engine run.

At a picnic in the hills, sun on the grass, Stu lifted a rock and brought it down on a young woman's skull.

That evening the tremor came, shaking windows and glasses and telephone lines across the whole city, and the news gathered every death, every wreck, every quiet unraveling into a single broadcast, delivered calmly, as if it were only weather.

The car came out of nowhere, or Ruben's Nova did, blowing the red at the junction with such speed that Celine Vaz never saw the color of the light, only the sudden white bloom of the windshield and the sound of her own leg breaking somewhere below her knowledge of pain.

Before that, months before, Ruben had lived in a cramped house with his mother, his brother Nestor, Nestor's wife Alma, and their baby, all of them breathing the same thin air. Nestor came home smelling of a robbed pharmacy and put his hands on Alma the way he put his hands on everything he thought he owned, and Ruben began to whisper to her that they could leave, that there was a way out that didn't run through his brother's fists.

He found the way out in a dog. Nestor's rottweiler, Tigre, killed other dogs on sight, and Ruben, seeing money where his brother saw a nuisance, began entering him in the pits behind the warehouses. Tigre won. Tigre kept winning.

Ruben paid two men to break Nestor's ribs in an alley, thinking it would loosen his grip on the house, on Alma. Instead Nestor gathered up Alma, the baby, and every peso of Ruben's hidden savings, and vanished into the city like smoke going up a flue.

The last fight ended with the promoter Chaco putting a bullet in Tigre for costing him money, and Ruben burying a knife in Chaco's side before running into the night with his friend Pipo, the dog left broken in the dirt behind them.

Nestor turned up again only to die, shot through the chest robbing a bank he'd chosen badly. At the funeral Ruben made his last offer, the same one he'd made a hundred times — come with me, leave this life — and Alma looked at him over the casket and said no, and meant it.

Across the city, in another life entirely, Celine's lover Hector had already left his wife and daughters for her, moving her into a flat that faced her own enormous image on a billboard, forty feet of her own face watching her undress every night.

She woke from the crash in a hospital bed, her leg pinned with steel, and the first thing she asked for was her lapdog Chispa, who was lost somewhere in the unfamiliar rooms of the new flat.

Chispa fell through a gap in the floorboards chasing some smell only dogs can name, and Hector tore up the boards with his hands while Celine's leg blackened past saving in its cast.

They took the leg below the knee. They took the billboard down not long after — replaced by a phone company, her forty-foot face folded into a truck and driven off to be recycled.

Meanwhile a businessman named Elian hired a vagrant named Cardo — once a guerrilla, now a killer for money — to end his half-brother Sergio, who was also his partner and, in Elian's ledger, his enemy.

Cardo had watched, weeks earlier, from behind a fence as they buried the wife he'd left decades before, then followed his grown daughter Perla home without knocking, without speaking, just to see the shape of the life he'd abandoned.

It was Cardo who had knelt at the wreck of Ruben's crash, dragging the bleeding rottweiler from the twisted door before the ambulances came, some old instinct pulling him toward the thing that was still fighting to live.

He nursed the dog through weeks in his own yard, among his own pack of strays, feeding it by hand until Tigre's ribs stopped showing.

Then one night, left alone, Tigre killed every other dog in that yard, and Cardo stood over him afterward with a pistol against the dog's skull and found he could not make his finger move.

He took Sergio instead of killing him, chained him in the ruin where he slept, unable to finish what Elian was paying for.

He brought the brothers face to face at last, set a single loaded gun on the table between them, and walked out having taken money from both men, letting them decide what blood was worth.

Then he went to Perla's flat one final time, let himself in, and left a long confession on her answering machine — who he was, what he'd done, why he'd watched from the fence — and took her photograph from the mantel before he left.

In the morning he shaved, put on clean clothes, left every peso he had folded on her table, and walked out into the wasteland at the edge of the city with Tigre beside him, the two of them disappearing into the flat grey light together.

In the bar, two years afterwards, Odile told Wilder that her marriage was over. She said it without drama, the way one reports a train delayed rather than cancelled, and added that she had spent the previous night confessing everything to her husband—every rented afternoon, every excuse, the whole small architecture of it laid bare on their kitchen table while he listened and said almost nothing.

Then, because she had never learned to leave a confession clean, she let slip that Emlyn had for some time been publishing a writer whom Wilder represented, a man both of them quietly detested for his adjectives and his ambitions. She said it lightly, as though it were merely one more coincidence in a life that had run out of them.

Wilder rang Emlyn that same hour, his voice too even, asking would he come round. Emlyn came, that evening, hat still on when he stepped through the door, as if the visit were an errand rather than a reckoning.

He said he had known for four years. He said his wife had told him on the trip abroad, in the hotel with the wallpaper the colour of weak tea, and that he had taken the news the way one takes a hand at cards one already suspects is lost. He said, too, that he had never thought much of Wilder's letters either—the ones from Odile's drawer, the ones he'd once glimpsed the return address of at a hotel desk—flat things, he said, poorly written for a man in his position.

Before any of that, though—chronologically behind them now, but rising up out of memory in no order at all—there had been the end of the rented rooms: the crockery divided between two string bags, the lease surrendered to a landlord who barely looked up from his ledger, the whole arrangement folded away like a table no longer needed.

Before that, dinner at the married couple's house, the two men discussing racquet games, the exact angle of a serve, some boy they'd both known at school who had gone on to nothing, while Odile sat between them with no part in the talk at all, her fork moving without appetite.

Before that, the hotel abroad, the letter waiting at the desk in a hand Emlyn recognised too well, and his mild question about who might be writing to his wife in that particular slant.

Before that, her confession, delivered without tears, and his answer—that he had always been fonder of his friend than of her, said not as cruelty but as fact, the kind one states about weather.

Before that, she had gone back to the rented rooms and said nothing about the trip, and the afternoon had passed exactly as the others had, tea poured at the same hour, the clock making its ordinary noise.

Before that, a long lunch, Emlyn and Wilder drinking through it, Emlyn baiting him about contemporary fiction, its thinness, its borrowed feelings, never once mentioning what he had learned, as if the knowledge were a coin he preferred to keep in his pocket rather than spend.

Earlier still, the rooms themselves, filled with linen and plates, a small household built for an affair that wanted the dignity of furniture.

And earlier than that, her announcement that she was carrying her husband's child, and their strange, quiet decision that the rooms should go on exactly as before, as though a pregnancy were weather to be waited out rather than a door closing.

And first of all, before any of it had hardened into habit, the party at Emlyn's house, Wilder leading her up the stairs away from the noise of glasses below, telling her—in the particular hush of a room not their own—how lovely she was, while beneath them the ordinary evening continued, ice dropped into glasses, someone's laugh rising and falling, none of them yet aware how long the arrangement above their heads would run, or how quietly it would end.

He became unstuck the day they made him a chaplain's assistant, though he would not have called it that yet, and shipped him overseas with nothing in his kit but a Bible and a false sense of purpose. That was one place he existed. Another was a zoo enclosure on a planet whose name he never learned to pronounce correctly, glass on all sides, a film actress reclining nearby on a chaise the aliens had built from a photograph in a magazine they'd stolen off a satellite. He did not experience these in order. He experienced them.

He was born in a small industrial town, weak-chested, odd-eyed, the kind of child who is teased for the way he stands. He grew up there and did not grow up straight.

He was housed, later or earlier, in a disused abattoir in a great city, sleeping on hooks' shadows with other prisoners, the smell of old blood in the concrete no one could scrub out.

He was hospitalized after the war, thin as paper, and it was there, in a ward that smelled of iodine, that another patient introduced him to a hack writer of science fiction who talked about time as if it were a road you could walk backward on.

The aliens explained it best, actually, lounging behind their glass, indifferent to his human urgency: every moment already exists, they said, all of it laid out like a landscape, and free will was a parochial superstition of his species alone.

He was lost behind the lines with a scout who hated him, who beat him when he begged to be left in the snow to die.

He married the daughter of the man who owned the optometry school, and money came to him the way rain comes to a place that has flooded before — too much, all at once, without asking whether he wanted it.

The city burned in one night while he slept in the meat locker with the others, and they climbed up into daylight to find nothing where the spires had been, only smoke standing in for buildings.

His daughter, much later, decided he had gone senile, that the stories about aliens and the fourth dimension were the ravings of a man no longer fit to run his own affairs, and she took them from him gently, the way you take a knife from a child.

His father had thrown him into the deep end of a pool once, believing the shock of drowning was how boys learned to swim, and he had only sunk, arms limp, watching the light bend far above him.

The scout died of gangrene on the prison train, and used his last breath to name him as the cause of everything, every mile, every wrong turn.

He went on the radio, years on, and tried to explain the aliens, the zoo, the fourth dimension, the way time sat still while men mistook their walking through it for change. The host grew impatient. The switchboard lit up with calls from people who thought he was a lunatic or a prophet, no in-between.

The prisoners were made to dig bodies from the cellars after the fire, clawing through ash and timber, until one of the diggers vomited air itself, having nothing left inside him, and died of it.

He survived an air crash in the mountains, walked out with a broken collarbone and a strange calm, and his wife, driving to meet him at the hospital, died breathing the fumes of her own idling car in a closed garage.

He was held in a camp beside enemy officers who had been drawing double rations for years through some clerk's forgotten error, growing fat while the rest of them grew thin.

He was shot dead by a beam of light after addressing a crowd from a stage, exactly as he had always known he would be, because he had already lived that moment the way he had lived all of them, out of order, all at once.

He became unstuck the day they made him a chaplain's assistant, though he would not have called it that yet, and shipped him overseas with nothing in his kit but a Bible and a false sense of purpose. That was one place he existed. Another was a zoo enclosure on a planet whose name he never learned to pronounce correctly, glass on all sides, a film actress reclining nearby on a chaise the aliens had built from a photograph in a magazine they'd stolen off a satellite. He did not experience these in order. He experienced them.

He was born in a small industrial town, weak-chested, odd-eyed, the kind of child who is teased for the way he stands. He grew up there and did not grow up straight.

He was housed, later or earlier, in a disused abattoir in a great city, sleeping on hooks' shadows with other prisoners, the smell of old blood in the concrete no one could scrub out.

He was hospitalized after the war, thin as paper, and it was there, in a ward that smelled of iodine, that another patient introduced him to a hack writer of science fiction who talked about time as if it were a road you could walk backward on.

The aliens explained it best, actually, lounging behind their glass, indifferent to his human urgency: every moment already exists, they said, all of it laid out like a landscape, and free will was a parochial superstition of his species alone.

He was lost behind the lines with a scout who hated him, who beat him when he begged to be left in the snow to die.

He married the daughter of the man who owned the optometry school, and money came to him the way rain comes to a place that has flooded before — too much, all at once, without asking whether he wanted it.

The city burned in one night while he slept in the meat locker with the others, and they climbed up into daylight to find nothing where the spires had been, only smoke standing in for buildings.

His daughter, much later, decided he had gone senile, that the stories about aliens and the fourth dimension were the ravings of a man no longer fit to run his own affairs, and she took them from him gently, the way you take a knife from a child.

His father had thrown him into the deep end of a pool once, believing the shock of drowning was how boys learned to swim, and he had only sunk, arms limp, watching the light bend far above him.

The scout died of gangrene on the prison train, and used his last breath to name him as the cause of everything, every mile, every wrong turn.

He went on the radio, years on, and tried to explain the aliens, the zoo, the fourth dimension, the way time sat still while men mistook their walking through it for change. The host grew impatient. The switchboard lit up with calls from people who thought he was a lunatic or a prophet, no in-between.

The prisoners were made to dig bodies from the cellars after the fire, clawing through ash and timber, until one of the diggers vomited air itself, having nothing left inside him, and died of it.

He survived an air crash in the mountains, walked out with a broken collarbone and a strange calm, and his wife, driving to meet him at the hospital, died breathing the fumes of her own idling car in a closed garage.

He was held in a camp beside enemy officers who had been drawing double rations for years through some clerk's forgotten error, growing fat while the rest of them grew thin.

He was shot dead by a beam of light after addressing a crowd from a stage, exactly as he had always known he would be, because he had already lived that moment the way he had lived all of them, out of order, all at once.

And the prisoner who'd sworn to have him killed one day, on the dead scout's account, only smiled when he heard, as if a debt long overdue had finally, at some point in the tangled architecture of time, been paid.
